items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Erroll Garner had Don Byas, Slam and Specs Powell in a quartet.

ctx.x: We heard that Mary Lou had been offered a job at Kelly's Stable for the trio at a salary of five-hundred dollars a week. Al and I were expecting to get a hundred and fifty a week and Mary Lou would have two-hundred because she was the leader of the trio arranger. But nothing happened and we never knew if the rumour was true because we didn't ask Mary Lou about the deal. So we were rehearsing with no work in view and the trio drifted apart. Later I heard that we were supposed to have gone into the 'Downbeat Club'…

Mildred Bailey was featuring one or two known musicians on her weekly show and as she knew me, I was asked to do a number one week. I wanted to do "Russian Lullaby" and asked Mary Lou to make a lead sheet of the arrangement we had recorded for the staff arranger of Mildred's show. When the day came for the rehearsal, Al had seen his part of the music and told me that it was not arranged in the key we recorded it in which was 'C' for the piano, and the arrangement was in 'F'. The director of the orchestra was Paul…
Came Christmas and the New Year of 1945, and John Kirby contacted me for a gig. There were a few changes from the original musicians

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: The text mentions Gordon 'Specs' Powell as part of Eddie South's orchestra in a descriptive passage about the club's lineup, but the interviewee does not explicitly state a personal interaction or relationship with Powell.

ctx.x: The club featured Teddy Wilson and Eddie South's orchestra, the Gates, the Boogies without Joe Turner, Hazel Scott and a comedian named Penner. Eddie South was a violinist known as "the Dark Angel" of that instrument and had been trained by some of the finest violin professors in Europe and especially in Hungaria. He was a classical musician that could play jazz also and had recorded some duets with the famous Stephane Grappelly in France.

Eddie had the bassist Dole Dickens, a fine classical and jazz pianist named Stanley Facey and the well known drummer Gordon "Specs" Powell to accompany him. Eddie was one of the attractions in the floor show and also played for dancing when we had our intermissions.

The club jumped from the opening night on and the clientele (customers) was of a higher society class than that at the downtown club which was in the Village, a part of New York that was considered to be the little Paris in the Apple, at least the left bank of Paris.
